title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The weather was already turning wintry and morning frosts hardened the earth, which was saturated from autumn rains. The green of the pastures stood out sharply against the brownish strips of winter rye trampled by cattle, and against the pale yellow stubble of the spring buckwheat. The wooded ravines and copses, still green islands amid the black fields and stubble at the end of August, had turned to golden and crimson islands amid the green winter rye. The hares had already half changed their summer coats, the fox cubs were beginning to scatter, and the young wolves were bigger than dogs. It was the best time of year for the hunt. The hounds of the passionate young sportsman Rostov had not only reached peak winter condition but were so worn out that at a meeting of the huntsmen it was decided to give them three days' rest and then, on the sixteenth of September, to set out on a distant expedition to the oak grove where there was an undisturbed litter of wolf cubs.

All that day the hounds stayed home. It was frosty and the air was sharp, but toward evening the sky clouded over and it began to thaw. On the fifteenth, when young Rostov in his dressing gown looked out the window, he saw the morning was perfect for hunting: the sky seemed to be melting and sinking earthward with no wind at all. The only movement in the air was the slow fall of microscopic droplets of drizzling mist. The bare twigs in the garden were hung with transparent drops that fell on the freshly fallen leaves. The earth in the kitchen garden looked wet and black and glistened like poppy seeds, merging at a short distance into the dull, moist veil of fog. Nicholas went out onto the wet, muddy porch. There was a smell of rotting leaves and of dog. Milka, a black-spotted, broad-haunched bitch with prominent dark eyes, got up on seeing her master, stretched her hind legs, crouched like a hare, and then suddenly leaped up and licked him right on the nose and mustache. Another borzoi, catching sight of his master from the garden path, arched his back and, rushing headlong toward the porch with tail raised, began rubbing himself against his legs.

"O-hoy!" came that inimitable huntsman's call at that moment — the one that blends the deepest bass with the shrillest treble — and around the corner came Daniel, the head huntsman and chief kennelman: a gray, wrinkled old man with hair cut straight across his forehead in the Ukrainian style, a long bent whip in his hand, and that look of independence and scorn for everything that is only found in huntsmen. He doffed his Circassian cap to his master and looked at him contemptuously. This contempt was not offensive to his master. Nicholas knew that this Daniel, who looked down on everyone and considered himself above all of them, was still his serf and his huntsman.

"Daniel!" Nicholas said timidly, conscious at the sight of the weather, the hounds, and the huntsman that he was being swept away by that irresistible passion for the hunt that makes a man forget all his previous resolutions, as a lover forgets everything in the presence of his beloved.

"What are your orders, your excellency?" said the huntsman in his deep bass — deep as a deacon's and hoarse from years of halloing — as two flashing black eyes gazed from beneath his brows at his master, who was saying nothing. "Can you resist it?" those eyes seemed to ask.
"Good day for it, eh? For a hunt and a gallop, eh?" asked Nicholas, scratching Milka behind the ears.
Daniel didn't answer, but winked instead.

"I sent Uvarka out at dawn to listen," his deep voice boomed after a minute's pause. "He says she's moved them into the Otradnoe enclosure. They were howling there." This meant that the she-wolf they both knew about had moved with her cubs into the Otradnoe copse, a small wood about a mile and a half from the house.
"We ought to go, don't you think?" said Nicholas. "Come to me with Uvarka."
"As you wish."
"Then hold off feeding them."
"Yes, sir."

Five minutes later Daniel and Uvarka were standing in Nicholas's large study. Though Daniel was not a big man, seeing him in a room was like seeing a horse or a bear among the furniture and trappings of human life. Daniel felt this himself, and as usual stood just inside the door, trying to speak softly and keep still for fear of breaking something in the master's apartment. He rushed to say everything necessary so he could get out from under that ceiling, back into the open air under the sky.

Having finished his questions and extracted from Daniel the opinion that the hounds were fit — Daniel himself wanted to go — Nicholas ordered the horses saddled. But just as Daniel was about to leave, Natasha came in with quick steps, her hair not done up and her old nurse's big shawl wrapped around her. Petya ran in at the same moment.
"You're going?" asked Natasha. "I knew you would! Sonya said you wouldn't, but I knew that today was the kind of day you couldn't resist."

"Yes, we're going," replied Nicholas reluctantly, for today he planned to hunt seriously and didn't want to bring Natasha and Petya along. "We're going, but only after wolves — it would be dull for you."
"You know it's my greatest pleasure," said Natasha. "It's not fair — you're going off by yourself, having the horses saddled, and you didn't even tell us."
"'No barrier bars a Russian's path' — we're going!" shouted Petya.
"But you can't. Mama said you mustn't," said Nicholas to Natasha.
"Yes, I'll go. I'm definitely going," said Natasha firmly. "Daniel, tell them to saddle up for us, and have Michael come with my dogs," she added to the huntsman.

It seemed irksome and improper to Daniel to be in a room at all, but to deal with a young lady struck him as simply impossible. He lowered his eyes and hurried out as if it were none of his business, careful not to cause any accidental harm to the young lady.
